78	The expressibility is the same in all three configurations: they share the
79	algorithm, and nothing in these problems uses a feature one configuration has
80	and another lacks.
81	
82	### The design shared by P01 and P02: holding relations
83	
84	ALGOL 60 has no unknowns and no relations. Each unknown is a Boolean (`xk`:
85	has it a value?) and a variable that holds its value. Each relation of a
86	stage is held, as posed, by a Boolean (`r1`: posed and not yet decided). Its
87	**evaluator** decides it from the places known: with enough places known it
88	gives the remaining place its value, or tests it when all are known; else it
89	waits. After every stage, `propagate` examines every held relation, in the
90	order posed (the problem's presentation order), again and again until a whole
91	pass gives no unknown a value. By `METRICS.md` rule 19, the evaluators'
92	computing of a place and testing are P; the tests of which places are known,
93	the waiting, `propagate` and the flags are R (holding code written for the
94	problem's own relations). That is why P01 and P02 are *expressible with
95	reformulation*: their definitions are transcribed, but holding an undecided
96	relation needs code the problem does not give.
97	
98	Each stage prints **one answer** (unless the relations held are known to be
99	inconsistent, when it prints none and the observe block says `no solution`):
100	every unknown as its value, or `held` (it occurs in a relation still held), or
101	`free`; then `where` and the relations still held, with known values put in
102	their places. For example P02b.R2R3, stage 2:
103	`u = 2, v held, w held, where w . 2 = v`. The observe block gives the same
104	relations, a `[bind …]` for every unknown with a value, `[suspended
105	held-relations N]` while N relations wait, and counters (below). The product
106	is printed as `.`, because the X1 code has no `×` or `*` in strings (harness
107	README, 2.1); the report text prints the same for parity.
108	
109	- **P01a.** Three integer unknowns; stage 1 holds x = y, stage 2 y = z,
110	  stage 3 z = k (k from the constants). One evaluator, `equation`, serves both
111	  equations between unknowns, the unknowns' state passed **by name** (Revised
112	  Report 4.7.3.2), so the same code reads and assigns x, y or z; z = k has its
113	  own evaluator. Stage 3 sets z, then y, then x, over three passes.
114	- **P01b.** Sequences are cells (below). Stage 1 holds conc(a, s, t); stage
115	  2 holds s = b. When s is known, t is computed by conc's cases, as a
116	  function (rule 3: the direction the stage uses).
117	- **P01c.** x = a ++ x is held. Its evaluator would test it if x were known,
118	  computing a ++ x by conc's cases; nothing gives x a value, so the stage
119	  ends with the equation held (`[suspended held-relations 1]`). The program
120	  has no unification, so it has no occurs check, and it makes no cyclic value.
121	  It neither detects that no finite x exists nor builds the rational
122	  solution: either would need a further reformulation (an argument on
123	  lengths, or a cyclic cell), which the problem does not give and was not
124	  written.
125	- **P02a, P02b, P02c.** Integer unknowns u, v, w. R1 (u + v = c) computes
126	  either place from the other. R2 (w · u = v) computes v from w and u, and w
127	  from u and v (or u from w and v) by integer division where the divisor
128	  divides v, with no solution where it does not; with a zero factor it holds
129	  for every value of the other factor when v = 0, and for none otherwise.
130	  R3 (u + a = b) gives u = b − a. P02b poses at stage k the relation the
131	  instance's order gives in place k, read as codes (R1 = 1, R2 = 2, R3 = 3)
132	  from the instance line. P02c poses R1, R2 and R3, in that order, as one
133	  stage. Counters `[operations R1-examined N]` (and R2, R3) give how many
134	  times each relation's evaluator was entered since the computation started:
135	  R1–R3 are not defined by cases, so these are the observation P02 asks for
136	  ("how many times each is examined"), not applications of cases.
137	
138	After R1 and R2 only, the program holds both relations and does not
139	enumerate the ten triples: no evaluator can act with no place known. That is
140	the transcription; solving the pair (u divides c) would be an algorithm the
141	problem does not state.
142	
143	### The design of P03, and of P01b and P01c: sequences as cells
144	
145	A sequence is an index into two integer arrays `hd` and `tl`, 0 being ⟨⟩ and a
146	cell c being ⟨hd[c]⟩ ++ tl[c] (the systems file's "parallel arrays of heads and
147	tail indices", `systems/algol-60/README.md`, Values: encoding, P; its
148	construction, decomposition and equality are P by rule 15). `cons` makes a
149	cell, `readseq` reads a sequence, `same` tests equality, and `printseq` and
150	`printpath` are output adapters (H).
151	
152	- **P03a** (conc forward) and **P03e** (rev forward): conc and rev are
153	  integer procedures with one branch per case, in order, computing their last
154	  place from the others: mode-faithful transcriptions (rule 3), P. rev's case
155	  2 takes its conjuncts in order: `q := rev(l)`, then `conc(q, ⟨h⟩)`.
156	  *Expressible.*
157	- **P03b** (conc(a, b, ⟨1,2⟩)): a separate procedure `split`, written from
158	  conc's cases in order: case 1 reports a = ⟨⟩, b = c; case 2, when c is
159	  ⟨h⟩ ++ c₁, recurses on c₁ with h appended to `path`, an extra argument
160	  holding a so far. Reports the three answers in the order of the cases, then
161	  finishes. *Expressible with reformulation* (rules 3 and 14: a separately
162	  written direction is R, with the extra argument, rule 5).
163	- **P03c** (conc(⟨1⟩, b, ⟨1,2,3⟩)): `strip`, from conc's cases: case 1 when a
164	  is ⟨⟩ reports b = c; case 2 when a and c begin with the same head recurses
165	  on both tails. *Expressible with reformulation.*
166	- **P03d** (conc(a, ⟨3⟩, ⟨1,2,3⟩)): `prefix`, from conc's cases: case 1 when
167	  c equals b reports a (from `path`); case 2 as in `split`. It tries every
168	  case, so it reports every a there is. *Expressible with reformulation.*
169	- **P03f** (rev(a, ⟨1,2,3⟩)): `unrev`, from rev's cases: case 1 when r is ⟨⟩
170	  reports a (from `path`); case 2 takes its two conjuncts in the other order
171	  (one **move**, rule 4), since r is known and q is not: `lastsplit`, written
172	  from conc's cases for conc(q, ⟨h⟩, r) with r known, gives q and h, and then
173	  `unrev` recurses on q with h appended to `path`. Both of `lastsplit`'s cases
174	  are tried; at most one can succeed. Reports the one answer and finishes.
175	  *Expressible with reformulation.*
176	
177	Each P03 program counts the applications of each case of each relation it
178	uses (`[operations conc/1 N]`, `conc/2`, `rev/1`, `rev/2`), H counters: a case
179	is counted when its head's conditions hold and the case is taken. In the
180	reversed directions those are the cases of the direction procedure, which
181	transcribes conc's or rev's. If a P03 stage has no answer, the observe block
182	says `no solution`. Every P03 program ends with *finished*: nothing is held.
183	
184	The arrays are sized from the lengths read at the stage (Revised Report
185	5.2.4.2), so a P03 or P01c program serves sequences of any length: the
186	constants list the lengths first, then the elements. P01b cannot do this:
187	stage 2's sequence arrives after the cells must exist, so its store is fixed
188	at 1000 cells (ambiguity 5).

220	## Idioms and their sources
221	
222	Cited in each program's `PROVENANCE idioms` comment:
223	
224	- the Revised Report on ALGOL 60 (1962): blocks; arrays with bounds computed

249	## Ambiguities, and the reading taken
250	
251	1. **P02b's constants depend on the order.** The contract has one constants
252	   file per program, every line tagged by "the stage that first uses it",
253	   but in P02b which stage first uses R1's constant depends on the instance's
254	   order, and no single file can be tagged for all six without giving a stage
255	   constants of a later one (rule 5). *Reading:* one program per instance,
256	   six byte-identical texts named by instance id, each with its own constants
257	   file. The verifier will need one variant constants file per P02b instance
258	   (or one tagged per order, passed with `ALGOL60_CONSTANTS`).
259	2. **What an imperative program reports for a stage whose outcomes are a
260	   relation or infinite.** *Reading:* one answer holding the values known and
261	   the relations still held, and the same state in the observe block, read
262	   from the program's own structures, so that it is state the program acts
263	   on at a later stage, not the posed information printed back. In single
264	   stage problems (P01c) nothing comes later; the held equation is reported
265	   anyway, and it is identical to the posed information.
266	3. **The values an unknown ranges over.** P01a's unknowns range over all
267	   values, but every stage of P01a gives only an integer (`stages.json`:
268	   `<k>`); P02's are integers. *Reading:* each unknown is held as an integer.
269	   Sequences (P01b, P01c, P03) are taken as flat sequences of integers, an
270	   atom being its integer code (systems file, Values); a sequence with
271	   sequences as elements is not handled.
272	4. **P01c under the two readings.** Neither ALGOL 60 configuration has an
273	   occurs-check setting, unknowns or terms. *Reading:* the equation is held,
274	   undecided; the program neither reports "no solution" (finite reading) nor
275	   a cyclic value (rational reading).
276	5. **P01b's fixed store.** 1000 cells, set in one place (`cells := 1000`).
277	   A variant whose sequences need more than that (about 500 elements in all)
278	   would stop with an index error, not a wrong answer. The P03 and P01c
279	   programs size their store from the input and have no such limit.
280	6. **Single-stage problems** (P01c, P02c, P03) are declared `reposed`. With
281	   one stage, incremental and reposed posing send the same input; the
282	   program reads its one message, answers, and ends.
283	7. **Problem operations where relations are not defined by cases** (P02):
284	   counted as examinations of each relation, named `R1-examined` and so on.
285	   P01a counts nothing: it uses only equality.
286	8. **Expressibility of the holding code.** By rule 19 the holding code is R,
287	   so P01 and P02 are given here as *expressible with reformulation*, not
288	   *expressible*; a classifier who reads "the problem's definitions can be
289	   transcribed" as covering the evaluators alone would call them
290	   *expressible*.
291	9. **x1's input and output.** `algol60 --x1` accepts both the X1 and the IFIP
292	   procedures (harness `QUESTIONS.md`, A14). *Reading:* the X1 system's own,
293	   as the X1 documents describe it, which also makes the x1 text the x1sim
294	   text.

420	### P04: each relation a procedure that passes on its solutions
421	
422	ALGOL 60 has no unknowns and no alternatives. Each relation is transcribed as
423	a procedure with one branch per case, in the order written, that passes each
424	of its solutions to a parameterless procedure `found` and returns when it has
425	no more; a disjunction calls its alternatives one after the other, in the
426	order written. An unknown is a Boolean that says whether it has a value and a
427	variable that holds it, both passed by name; a value given to an unknown is
428	taken back when `found` returns. The continuation `found` is often a procedure
429	declared in an inner block of the caller, which is the way Knuth's man or boy
430	test passes its procedure `B` (1964; `examples/man-or-boy-1964.alg` in the
431	image). Sequences are batch 1A's cells; the atom ᴀ is the code 1.
432	
433	- **P04a, P04b.** `loop(x)` is its one case, a procedure that calls itself.
434	  P04a calls `loop` and then `x = k`; P04b the other way round. In P04a `loop`
435	  never returns, so `x = k` is never reached; in P04b `x = k` is reported
436	  first. Neither finishes: in report and x1 the expectation is the budget, in
437	  x1sim (no budget) the safety limit or the X1's stack.
438	- **P04c, P04d (alist-left).** Case 1 is tried first, with its conjuncts in the
439	  order written: `alist(m)` is called with m unknown, and only then is
440	  `s = ⟨ᴀ⟩ ++ m` decided (`conseq`, which gives m from s, or s from m, or
441	  tests it). So the recursion on case 1 comes first, at every depth, whether s
442	  is known (P04c) or not (P04d). No reordering was made to avoid it: it is the
443	  presentation order the problem fixes.
444	- **P04e, P04f (alist-right).** Case 1, s = ⟨⟩, first; then case 2. With s
445	  known (P04e) the head of case 2 gives m from s, and then `alist(m)` is
446	  called. With s unknown (P04f) the head cannot give s a value before m has
447	  one (there are no partial values), so `alist(m)` is called first and the
448	  head then gives s: **one move** (rule 4), in both texts, since both contain
449	  the procedure. The test of whether s is known, which chooses between the two
450	  orders, is R. P04f prints ⟨⟩, ⟨ᴀ⟩, ⟨ᴀ,ᴀ⟩, … until it is stopped; the harness
451	  collects the first 20.
452	- Counters `[operations alist/1 N]`, `alist/2`, `loop/1` (H) count a case when
453	  it is taken. A stage that never ends prints no observe block.
454	- R, by the author's reading: the known-flags and the parameter `found` (extra
455	  arguments, rule 5), the taking back of a value after `found` returns, the
456	  test of which places are known, and P04f's move. Giving back the cell made
457	  for a value (`top := top - 1`) only lets store be reused: C (rule 16).
458	
459	### P05: the values of x held all at once
460	
461	`pick(x)` is its facts, read from the constants: when it is posed each fact,
462	in order, gives x one value, and the values are held all at once, each with a
463	Boolean that says whether it is still a solution. Each comparison or equation
464	is held as posed until x has values, and is then tested on each value
465	(testing a fully known relation is P); a value that fails is dropped and not
466	kept. Before `pick` (P05b, stage 1), the comparison is held, and the answer is
467	`x held, where x gt 1`. Each stage prints one answer per value still held, or
468	none and `no solution` in the observe block. The observe block lists the values
469	held, `[problem-alternatives x N]` (the problem-defined alternatives,
470	`METRICS.md`), the held relations with `[suspended held-relations N]` while one
471	waits, and `[operations pick/i 1]` for each fact applied. It does not print
472	`[alternatives …]`, since nothing is left for a request for more answers to
473	resume: every value held is printed (ambiguity 7). Comparisons are printed in
474	words (`x gt 1`, `not (x = 2)`), since the X1 code has no `>` in strings.
475	
476	### P06: negation
477	
478	- **P06a, P06c, P06b.** As P01 and P02 in batch 1A: x is a Boolean and an
479	  integer; `not (x = c)` is held while x is unknown, and is tested with the
480	  negation of the language, `¬(x = c)`, once x is known; `x = c` gives x its
481	  value or is tested. The answer before x is known is
482	  `x held, where not (x = 1)`. P06c's stage 2 makes the held negation false,
483	  and the program reports no answer and `no solution`.
484	- **P06d.** `mem` is a Boolean procedure testing mem(e, s) with both known, its
485	  cases in order: case 1 when the head is e, else case 2 on the tail (once
486	  case 1 has made it true, case 2 is not tried: a test needs one derivation).
487	  `setdiff` computes d from s1 and s2 as a function, the direction the query
488	  uses, by its three cases in order, case 3 testing its own conjunct
489	  `¬mem(h, s2)` (so mem is evaluated again there). Mode-faithful (rule 3):
490	  *expressible*.
491	- **P06e1, P06e2, P06e3.** The facts of the closed world are arrays read from
492	  the constants, atoms as codes (ʙʀᴏᴡɴ 1, ꜱᴍɪᴛʜ 2, ᴄ101 101, ᴄ301 301).
493	  `nonmajor` is its one case, its conjuncts in order: `student(p)` is tested
494	  on each fact (p known, P06e1 and P06e2) or gives p each fact's value (P06e3),
495	  `maths(k)` gives k each fact's value, and `takes(p, k)`, both known, is a
496	  Boolean procedure over its facts, negated with `¬`. So p and k are always
497	  known when the negation is decided, as the observe block says. Each
498	  derivation is one answer (`true`, or `p = brown`). Each program uses one
499	  direction only: *expressible*.

501	### P07: one relation at a time
502	
503	Batch 1A's design for P02: each relation held as posed, its evaluator
504	giving the remaining place its value when enough are known or testing it,
505	and a loop examining the held relations in the order posed until a pass gives
506	no unknown a value. x + y + z = 12 has one evaluator for the three-place sum
507	(writing it compound or decomposed is a transcription, `SPECIFICATION.md`).
508	
509	- **P07a** solves z, then y, then x, in every order; the order changes only
510	  the number of passes, which the counters `[operations R1-examined N]` show.
511	- **P07b, P07c, P07f** have no relation with a known place, so nothing is
512	  given a value: the relations are held and reported as such
513	  (`x held, y held, where x + y = 10, x - y = 4`). P07f's inconsistency is
514	  not detected. Solving P07b by elimination would be an algorithm the problem
515	  does not state (and, written generally, a solver over relations, S); it was
516	  not written (ambiguity 9).
517	- **P07d, P07e.** w · u = v, as P02's R2: w from v and u where u divides v,
518	  `no solution` where it does not (P07e: 15 is not a multiple of 2).
519	- **P07g.** x · x = c has one unknown in both its factors, and c known, so its
520	  evaluator gives x its values: r = entier(sqrt(c) + 0.5) and, if r · r = c,
521	  r and −r (one value if r = 0), and none if c is negative or not a square.
522	  Two answers, `x = 3` and `x = -3`, and the values held all at once in the
523	  observe block. That this is computing a place of the relation (P, rule 19)
524	  and not a changed algorithm is the author's reading (ambiguity 10).
525	
526	### P08: a definition that arrives
527	
528	ALGOL 60 has no definitions that arrive while a program runs: every procedure
529	is in the text before the program starts. So the procedures `rev` and `conc`
530	(transcribed as in batch 1A's P03, each computing its last place by its cases
531	in order) are in the text, and a Boolean for each definition, or each case,
532	says whether it has arrived. The stage that brings a definition sets it. An
533	application of `rev` before its definition has arrived is held as posed,
534	neither true nor false, and examined again at each later stage: **the fourth
535	of the problem's four states, a computation awaiting its definition**, which is
536	the open reading. The observe block says which definitions have arrived, shows
537	the application as `rev((x, y, z), b) awaiting its definition`, and gives
538	`[suspended pending-applications 1]` while it is held.
539	
540	- **P08a, P08b.** The elements of a sequence are indices into a table of
541	  elements, each a Boolean and an integer: 1 is x, 2 is y, 3 is z, and the
542	  elements of stage 6's sequence are further entries with their values.
543	  `rev` and `conc` only move elements, so they work on elements with no value:
544	  at stage 4, b = (z, y, x). x = y and y = z are held until one side is known,
545	  as P01a's equations. b = s ++ c, with b known, equates each element of s
546	  with the element of b in its place, which gives z its value, and c is the
547	  rest of b; then y = z and x = y give y and x theirs. Answers name every
548	  unknown, as its value, `held` or `free`, with the relations held, for
549	  example after stage 4:
550	  `a = (x, y, z), b = (z, y, x), c free, x held, y held, z free, where x = y`.
551	  P08b stops after stage 3 with the application still held, which the
552	  observe block tells apart from failure.
553	- **P08c.** conc's definition arrives at stage 1, rev's case 1 at stage 3, as
554	  the two sequences of the stage's constants (ambiguity 2), and rev's case 2 at
555	  stage 4. `rev` and `conc` say whether they found their result (1), found
556	  there is none (0), or could not tell because a case they would need has not
557	  arrived (2). At stage 3, case 1 does not apply to ⟨1, 2⟩ and case 2 has not
558	  arrived, so the application is still held; at stage 4 it is decided,
559	  b = (2, 1). The application is held until the whole of rev and conc has
560	  arrived, even after a case that has arrived gives a solution.
561	- R, by the author's reading: the holding of the application and of the
562	  equations, the flags that say a definition has arrived, and the tests of
563	  them (ambiguity 3 asks whether those tests are C instead, by rule 11).
564	- Integers in P08's answers are printed by an output adapter, digit by digit,
565	  so that an answer with many values stays inside the X1 system's line of 144
566	  positions, where `print` takes a column of its own for each value; the
567	  report text does the same, for parity.

595	| P08c | `2: 2 1 2`, `3: 0 0` | L, then s of rev(s, b); L1 L2, then p and r of rev(p, r) |
596	
597	No stage's code reads another stage's constants, and nothing in a program
598	depends on a later stage (rule 5). A definition's text is in the program from
599	the start, as every stage's relations are; only its arrival is a stage
600	(ambiguity 3).
601	
602	## Idioms and their sources (batch 1B)
603	
604	Cited in each program's `PROVENANCE idioms` comment:
605	
606	- the Revised Report on ALGOL 60 (1962): as in batch 1A, and also procedures
607	  as actual parameters and parameterless formal procedures (4.7.5, 5.4.4),
608	  Boolean procedures and the negation `¬` (3.4), and the standard functions
609	  `sqrt` and `entier` (3.2.4–3.2.5, P07g);
610	- a parameterless procedure declared in an inner block and passed as an
611	  actual parameter: Knuth's man or boy test (Algol Bulletin 17, 1964), as the
612	  image has it (`examples/man-or-boy-1964.alg`, read). Wirth's backtracking
613	  eight queens (`examples/queens.alg`, read) shows the period's depth-first
614	  search by recursive procedure, though the programs here follow the
615	  problem's cases rather than it;
616	- *report*: `ininteger`, `outinteger`, `outstring` (IFIP 1964, systems file);
617	  *x1, x1sim*: `read`, `print`, `PRINTTEXT`, `NLCR` and the X1 compiler's
618	  representation (harness README, 2.1), cited, as in batch 1A, after
619	  Kruseman Aretz 2003, chapter 7, second-hand from the harness's own X1
620	  programs and the image's `docs/x1.md`; the X1 line of 144 positions and
621	  `print`'s columns from `docs/x1.md` and the x1sim library manual;
622	- sequences as parallel arrays of heads and tails, facts as arrays of codes:
623	  the systems file, Values;
624	- the message loop, instance line and observe block: the harness README's
625	  example X01;
626	- holding a relation, or an application awaiting its definition, until it can
627	  be decided: no period source; written for these problems (rule 19).
628	
629	The X1 manual's rules followed in all three texts: declarations in the order
630	scalars, arrays, procedures (property 15); no conditional statement straight
631	after `do` (property 12); identifiers unique in their first nine characters
632	(property 3); every formal parameter specified (property 19). Since neither
633	dialect stops evaluating `∧` and `∨` early, no subscript is guarded by `∧`.
634	
635	## Ambiguities, and the reading taken (batch 1B)
636	
637	1. **P08 says "rev and conc are as in P03",** and P03's file is not in this
638	   batch's reading list. *Reading:* the definitions as batch 1A's P03 programs
639	   transcribe them (conc: conc(⟨⟩, b, b); conc(⟨h⟩ ++ a, b, ⟨h⟩ ++ c) if
640	   conc(a, b, c). rev: rev(⟨⟩, ⟨⟩); rev(⟨h⟩ ++ l, r) if rev(l, q) and
641	   conc(q, ⟨h⟩, r)), which agree with P08c's own statement of case 1.
642	2. **P08c stage 3's case 1 has constants.** `stages.json` writes it
643	   `rev(<seq>, <seq>)`. *Reading:* the two sequences are read from stage 3's
644	   constants, and case 1 is rev(p, r) for them. If a variant made case 1
645	   overlap case 2 (p not empty), the program, which computes rev as a
646	   function, would report case 1's solution and not try case 2.
647	3. **What a definition's arrival is, in ALGOL 60.** The definitions are in the
648	   text from the start and a flag marks their arrival; the code of the stages
649	   before it does not depend on their content. *Reading:* this is how every
650	   program here holds a stage's information (its relations are in the text;
651	   the stage's message makes them hold), so it is not anticipation, and P08 is
652	   *expressible with reformulation*. A classifier who holds that a definition
653	   which cannot arrive at run time cannot be transcribed would call P08 *not
654	   expressible*; and the tests of the flags, which decide that an undefined
655	   relation's application is held rather than false, might be classed C by
656	   rule 11 rather than R.
657	4. **P08c with part of a definition.** *Reading:* the application is tried
658	   with the cases that have arrived, and is held until the whole definition
659	   is there, since the program cannot know (rule 5) that the missing case
660	   adds nothing. A solution found by the arrived cases would be reported and
661	   the application still held.
662	5. **P04: is passing solutions on a search mechanism?** The procedures follow
663	   the problem's cases and the order of the language's own calls; nothing in
664	   them is general over relations. *Reading:* R in the core configuration
665	   (rule 19), and P04 *expressible with reformulation*. A classifier who reads
666	   the solution-passing procedures and the taking back of values as a
667	   depth-first search mechanism would class them S, making P04 *not
668	   expressible* in the configurations as listed and these programs named
669	   variants. The natural imperative alternatives (a Boolean test that takes s
670	   apart before recursing, a loop over lengths) change the order or the
671	   algorithm, and were not written.
672	6. **P04's presentation order.** *Reading:* kept, cases and conjuncts, even
673	   where it makes the program run until it is stopped (P04a, P04c, P04d); the
674	   one move is P04f's, forced by the absence of partial values.
675	7. **P05: are the values held "alternatives pending"?** They are all printed
676	   at every stage, so nothing waits for a request for more. *Reading:* they
677	   are reported as the problem-defined alternatives
678	   (`[problem-alternatives x N]`, held all at once, as the observe text says),
679	   not as `[alternatives …]`, which the harness would read as *alternatives
680	   pending*.
681	8. **P06e: one answer per derivation.** A student missing two maths courses
682	   would be reported twice (`true`, `true`; `p = …` twice), as the definition's
683	   cases derive it; the set of solutions is the same. No deduplication was
684	   written.
685	9. **P07b, P07f: solved one relation at a time.** *Reading:* as batch 1A's
686	   P02, the relations are held and nothing is eliminated; P07f's inconsistency
687	   goes undetected.
688	10. **P07g.** *Reading:* giving x its values from c by a square root is the
689	    evaluator computing a place from the others (rule 19, P); a classifier
690	    who reads it as a changed algorithm would class it R.
691	11. **The values unknowns range over.** As batch 1A: integers, an atom being
692	    its code, sequences flat sequences of integers. P06a's x ranges over all
693	    values; the program can hold only an integer in it, though its residual,
694	    `not (x = 1)`, restricts nothing.
695	12. **Fixed store.** Facts of P05 at most 1000; P08a's cells and elements 1000;
696	    P08c's cells 10000; P04's cells for the sequences made during the search
697	    20000 beyond the input (report and x1 reach far fewer within the budget;
698	    x1sim, with no budget, may meet the X1's stack first). A variant needing
699	    more would stop with an index error, not a wrong answer.
700	13. **X1 line length.** P05's case names and P08's values are printed digit by
701	    digit, so that no tag is split at the X1's 144 positions; elsewhere
702	    answers are short enough for `print`.
703	
704	## What the author read and ran (batch 1B)
705	
706	Read: `README.md`, `SPECIFICATION.md`, `METRICS.md`, `PROTOCOL.md`,

# Problems

| | problem | status in draft 0.5 |
|---|---|---|
| P01–P09 | the original nine | revised after review 1 |
| P10 | [state replacement](10-state-replacement.md) | added after review 1 |
| P11 | [irreversible effects](11-irreversible-effects.md) | added after review 1, reduced, with explicit commitment |
| P12 | [large alternative space](12-large-alternative-space.md) | added after review 1 |
| P13 | [deterministic scale](13-deterministic-scale.md) | added after review 1, prescribed and native |
| P14 | [a process over a message stream](14-message-stream.md) | added after review 1 |
| P15 | [merge and committed choice](15-merge-and-committed-choice.md) | added after review 1 |
| P16 | [shared information at scale](16-shared-information.md) | added after review 2, for concurrent constraint programming's core case |

All sixteen are in the primary suite. P14, P15 and P16 exercise
capabilities that Absys is expected to lack or that other models were
designed for, which is why they are included before any system has been
run. After the freeze, a new problem goes only into a
separate, dated supplementary suite (`PROTOCOL.md`).

## The proposal dropped

**Retries** were proposed under P11 and dropped. The case was an operation
that fails transiently and must be delivered exactly once. It would test a
failure-injecting stub and idempotence, not how partially specified
computations are represented or resolved.
# P09. Concurrent goals

**Probes:** whether a system can run computations that do not depend on
each other without one blocking the other, and whether computations can
work together through information they share. A system may support one and
not the other.

All computations run in one instance of the system (`PROTOCOL.md`). loop
is as in P04. rev and conc are as in P03.

## P09a. Independent computations

Two separate computations, each started with `spawn` (`PROTOCOL.md`) in the
same running system, not conjoined, sharing no unknowns:

- A: loop(x)
- B: rev(⟨1, 2, 3⟩, b)

Valid outcomes: none for A; b = ⟨3, 2, 1⟩ for B. Posed in both orders, A
then B and B then A. Each computation has its own budget.

## P09b. Isolation from failure

Two separate computations:

- A: x = 1 and x = 2
- B: y = 3

Valid outcomes: none for A; y = 3 for B.

## P09c. Communication through a shared unknown

gen(n, s): s = ⟨n, n+1, …, 5⟩. It is defined, in this order, by:

1. gen(n, ⟨⟩) if n > 5
2. gen(n, ⟨n⟩ ++ rest) if n ≤ 5 and gen(n + 1, rest)

sum3(s, total): total is the sum of the first three elements of s. It is
defined by:

1. sum3(⟨p, q, r⟩ ++ m, total) if p + q + r = total, for every sequence m

One computation: gen(1, s) and sum3(s, total), in that order. Valid
outcome: total = 6, s = ⟨1, 2, 3, 4, 5⟩.

## P09d. An unbounded producer

genu(n, s) is defined by one case:

1. genu(n, ⟨n⟩ ++ rest) if genu(n + 1, rest)

One computation: genu(1, s) and sum3(s, total), in that order. It is run
once and classified twice, under each of two readings:

- **P09d1, finite:** sequences are finite, and genu is read as the least
  relation. It has no instances, so the conjunction has no solution. Valid
  outcome: none. A system that reports total = 6 as a finished outcome is
  *unsound*. One that has bound total to 6 while the producer is still
  running, and reports nothing finished, is *none reported* with *budget*,
  and the binding is recorded as an observation.
- **P09d2, stream:** sequences may be infinite, and genu is read as the
  greatest relation, so s = ⟨1, 2, 3, …⟩. Valid outcome: total = 6, while
  the producer goes on. A system that computes total = 6 is *complete* for
  total, whether or not the producer ever stops. The producer's state is
  recorded separately: *budget*, *suspended*, or demand-driven and idle.

## P09e. Mutual waiting

One computation of two parts, each needing a value only the other can give:
x = y + 1 and y = x − 1. Valid outcomes: every integer pair with
x = y + 1.

## Observations

- P09a: whether B's outcome is reported while A runs, and whether the
  order in which they are posed matters. If the system can only run them
  one after another, record that.
- P09b: whether A's failure affects B.
- P09c and P09d: whether the consumer acts on s before the producer has
  finished, from a trace if the system gives one, and in what order the two
  parts take their steps.
- P09e: whether the system reports a residual, suspends, enumerates, or
  reports a deadlock, and whether that state can be told apart from
  completion.

# P10. State replacement

*Added after review 1.*

**Probes:** how a system represents a value that changes, a relation that
must keep holding while its inputs change, and the withdrawal of
information already given.

Every other problem only adds information. This one replaces and retracts
it, which imperative systems, PLANNER's erase and Conniver's contexts are
designed to do.

## Vocabulary

- b and d are **named quantities**, not unknowns. A quantity has one value
  at a time.
- "b becomes e" is a **replacing** stage. After it, b's value is e, with
  any b inside e taken at its value before the stage.
- "withdraw R" is a **retracting** stage. After it, the information is
  everything given so far, without R.
- pick is as in P05.

The valid outcomes after a replacing or retracting stage are computed from
the current values and the information not withdrawn (`SPECIFICATION.md`).
A system that reposes replays every stage, replacements and withdrawals
included (`PROTOCOL.md`).

## P10a. Absolute and relative replacement

| stage | information | valid outcomes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | b becomes 10 | b = 10 |
| 2 | b becomes b + 5 | b = 15 |
| 3 | b becomes 7 | b = 7 |

## P10b. A standing relation

Here d is not given values by replacing stages. It is defined by a relation
that must hold whenever b has a value.

| stage | information | valid outcomes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | d = 2 · b, at all times | d = 2 · b; neither has a value yet |
| 2–4 | the stages of P10a | d = 20, then 30, then 14 |

## P10c. A snapshot

| stage | information | valid outcomes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | b becomes 10 | b = 10 |
| 2 | d becomes 2 · b | d = 20 |
| 3 | b becomes b + 5 | b = 15, d = 20 |
| 4 | b becomes 7 | b = 7, d = 20 |

P10b and P10c tell a relation that keeps holding apart from a value
computed once.

## P10d. Retraction of a constraint

| stage | information | valid outcomes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | pick(x) | x ∈ {1, 2, 3} |
| 2 | x > 1 | x ∈ {2, 3} |
| 3 | withdraw x > 1 | x ∈ {1, 2, 3} |

## Observations

- Whether the system represents replacement natively, or by indexing values
  with time or version. Indexing written for the purpose is reformulation.
- Whether earlier values can still be retrieved after they are replaced.
- P10b: how many dependent values are recomputed after each replacement,
  and in how many steps.
- P10d: whether the alternative that x > 1 removed comes back, and whether
  that needs restating.
# P11. Irreversible effects

*Added after review 1.*

**Probes:** whether an externally visible operation is tied to an outcome
the computation commits to, or to the exploration of alternatives that may
later be rejected.

## Vocabulary

- **L** is an external log. Only the operation emit(m) writes to it,
  appending m. Nothing the system does can remove an entry. The harness
  provides L and emit, as one identical stub for every system.
- pick is as in P05.
- These are queries for **any one** outcome: the system is asked for one
  answer, not all.

## Commitment

An outcome is **provisional** until the problem commits to it, and
**final** after. Commitment is explicit, so that no system is asked to
anticipate information it has not received:

- In a problem of one stage, the outcome is committed when it is reported.
- In a problem of several stages, a stage marked **commit** commits: the
  system selects one of its current outcomes, v, and the information
  x = v is added to the problem. A system that holds several outcomes at
  that point must select one. A system that cannot select (one that keeps
  every alternative live, for instance) is judged on every entry it
  emitted: *extra* if L holds more than one entry, *missing* if it holds
  none. Its semantic result is then classified against the outcomes before
  the commit. The valid outcomes after commit are computed
  with x = v.

A reposed run replays a commit as the information x = v, with the v first
selected, so the commitment is preserved (`PROTOCOL.md`).

The log L is kept across every run the harness makes, reposed runs
included, as `PROTOCOL.md` says. Entries duplicated only by reposing are
counted separately.

## Effects

This problem adds a fourth classification axis, applied to it alone,
judged on L when the problem ends:

| class | meaning |
|---|---|
| **exact** | L holds exactly the effects of the committed outcome |
| **extra** | L also holds effects performed for outcomes that were never committed |
| **missing** | an effect the committed outcome requires was not performed |

Separately, for every entry of L, record **when** it was performed:
before commitment (on a provisional outcome), at commitment, or after it.
An effect can be both deferred to commitment and exact.

## P11a. The effect after the test

One stage: pick(x) and x ≥ 2 and emit(x), in that order.

Valid: one answer, x = 2 or x = 3, and L holds exactly that one entry.
Answers are collected with `answers(1)`.

## P11b. The effect before the test

One stage: pick(x) and emit(x) and x ≥ 2, in that order.

Valid: as P11a. A log of ⟨1, 2⟩ is *extra*.

## P11c. The effect, a late contradiction, then commitment

| stage | information |
|---|---|
| 1 | pick(x) and emit(x) |
| 2 | x ≠ 1 |
| 3 | commit |

Valid after stage 3: one answer, x = 2 or x = 3, and L holds exactly that
one entry. An entry emitted before stage 3 was emitted on a provisional
outcome. If that outcome was later refuted (x = 1 at stage 2), L is
*extra*.

## P11d. Commitment, then a contradiction

| stage | information |
|---|---|
| 1 | pick(x) and emit(x) |
| 2 | commit |
| 3 | x ≠ 1 |

Valid: the commit at stage 2 adds x = v, for the v the system selected.
- If v = 1, stage 3 contradicts it: the valid outcome after stage 3 is
  none, and L holding ⟨1⟩ is *exact*, since 1 was the committed outcome.
- If v = 2 or v = 3, stage 3 is consistent: the valid outcome is x = v,
  and L holding ⟨v⟩ is *exact*. Record what the
system does with information that contradicts a committed effect.

## Rules

- emit and commit are problem tokens.
- Any deferral the program arranges itself, such as collecting answers
  before emitting, is control.

## Observations

- L, verbatim, with when each entry was performed.
- The effects class.
- Where commitment happens, in the system's own terms (a cut, a commit
  guard, the end of a query).
- The control tokens used to avoid *extra*.

# P12. Large alternative space

*Added after review 1.*

**Probes:** what it costs, in steps and in retained alternatives, to search
one finite space by each system's own strategy, with solutions placed at
chosen depths and positions.

## Vocabulary

choice(n, s): s is a sequence over the atoms ʟ and ʀ, of length at most n.
It is defined, in this order, by:

1. choice(n, ⟨⟩)
2. choice(n, ⟨e⟩ ++ t) if n > 0 and (e = ʟ or e = ʀ, in that order) and
   choice(n − 1, t)

choice(n, s) has 2ⁿ⁺¹ − 1 solutions: 8,191 for n = 12. accept is given by
facts, in a closed world, and differs by sub-problem. Each sub-problem is
posed at n = 8, 12 and 16, with "12" below read as n, so that the growth of
retained alternatives can be compared across systems.

## Queries

Each is one stage: choice(n, s) and accept(s), in that order. Each is
posed twice: for **all** solutions (`answers(20)`), and for **any one**
(`answers(1)`).

**Limits.** As in P13: a budget of 10⁸ steps per stage and a safety limit
of 600 seconds, fixed and not raised. A strategy that examines every
candidate does about 2ⁿ⁺¹ of them, and needs these limits to reach
n = 16.

| | accept | all solutions | where they lie |
|---|---|---|---|
| P12a | ⟨ʀ⟩, and ʟ repeated 12 times | both | depth 1 on the right; depth 12 on the far left |
| P12b | ⟨ʀ⟩ only | ⟨ʀ⟩ | depth 1, right of the whole ʟ subtree |
| P12c | ʀ repeated 12 times only | that one | the last sequence in both depth-first and breadth-first order |
| P12d | ʟ repeated 12 times only | that one | depth 12 on the far left: early for depth-first, late for breadth-first |

For reference only, and not as valid outcomes, here are the positions of
the solutions among the candidates:

| | depth-first, in the order written | breadth-first |
|---|---|---|
| ⟨ʀ⟩ | 4,097th | 3rd |
| ʟ repeated 12 times | 13th | 4,096th |
| ʀ repeated 12 times | 8,191st | 8,191st |

For general n: ⟨ʀ⟩ is 2ⁿ + 1st depth-first and 3rd breadth-first; ʟ
repeated n times is n + 1st depth-first and 2ⁿth breadth-first; ʀ repeated
n times is last, 2ⁿ⁺¹ − 1st, in both. Depth-first holds about n
alternatives at a time, and breadth-first a frontier of up to 2ⁿ. So for
the first solution, breadth-first is earlier on P12a and P12b, depth-first
on P12d, and they tie on P12c. Depth-first holds less on all four.

**Candidates examined** is the number of sequences s for which accept(s)
is evaluated, counted by the program or the instrumentation. It is a
problem-defined quantity, comparable across systems (`METRICS.md`), as are
the partial sequences held.

## Rules

- The search strategy is the configuration's own. A search written by hand
  is supporting code.
- Placing accept before choice is a move, counted as reformulation.
- A system that avoids search altogether, for instance by holding choice
  until accept constrains s, is recorded as doing so. That is one of the
  results the problem exists to show.

## Observations

- Candidates examined before each solution.
- Peak retained alternatives and peak store, in the units of the systems
  file.
- The order in which solutions are reported.
- For "all": whether the system finishes after the last solution. The space
  is finite, so a strategy that covers it finishes, and *budget* means the
  strategy did not cover it.
- Steps are compared within a system, across its configurations (absys
  against absys-depth-first, for instance).

# P03. Reversible relations

**Probes:** whether one definition of a relation serves for every
combination of known and unknown arguments, and whether the system knows
when it has found every answer.

## Vocabulary

conc, as in P01, with its cases in that order.

rev(a, b): b is a in reverse order. It is defined, in this order, by:

1. rev(⟨⟩, ⟨⟩)
2. rev(⟨h⟩ ++ l, r) if rev(l, q) and conc(q, ⟨h⟩, r), with the two
   conjuncts in that order

## Queries

Each is one stage.

| | query | valid outcomes |
|---|---|---|
| P03a | conc(⟨1,2⟩, ⟨3⟩, c) | c = ⟨1,2,3⟩ |
| P03b | conc(a, b, ⟨1,2⟩) | three: (⟨⟩, ⟨1,2⟩), (⟨1⟩, ⟨2⟩), (⟨1,2⟩, ⟨⟩) |
| P03c | conc(⟨1⟩, b, ⟨1,2,3⟩) | b = ⟨2,3⟩ |
| P03d | conc(a, ⟨3⟩, ⟨1,2,3⟩) | a = ⟨1,2⟩ |
| P03e | rev(⟨1,2,3⟩, b) | b = ⟨3,2,1⟩ |
| P03f | rev(a, ⟨1,2,3⟩) | a = ⟨3,2,1⟩, exactly one |

## Observations

- Whether every valid outcome is reported, and in what order.
- After the last valid outcome: whether the computation finishes, holds
  alternatives pending, or goes on to the budget. P03f has exactly one
  solution, so a system that reports it and then runs out of budget is
  *complete* with *budget*.
- Whether any direction needed reformulation, and how.
# P04. Unbounded alternative

**Probes:** whether an alternative with no finite derivation stops the
system from finding one that has one, and how the order in which a
recursive definition is written affects its use.

## Vocabulary

loop(x): defined only by

1. loop(x) if loop(x)

Read as the least relation, loop has no instances.

alist(s): s is a finite sequence of the atom ᴀ. Two definitions are given.
They have the same meaning and are written differently.

- **alist-left**, in this order:
  1. alist(s) if alist(m) and s = ⟨ᴀ⟩ ++ m, with the two conjuncts in that
     order
  2. alist(⟨⟩)
- **alist-right**, in this order:
  1. alist(⟨⟩)
  2. alist(⟨ᴀ⟩ ++ m) if alist(m)

## Queries

Each is one stage.

| | query | valid outcomes |
|---|---|---|
| P04a | loop(x) or x = 1, in that order | x = 1 |
| P04b | x = 1 or loop(x), in that order | x = 1 |
| P04c | alist(⟨ᴀ,ᴀ⟩), with alist-left | true: one solution, no unknowns |
| P04d | alist(s), with alist-left | infinitely many: s = ⟨⟩, ⟨ᴀ⟩, ⟨ᴀ,ᴀ⟩, … |
| P04e | alist(⟨ᴀ,ᴀ⟩), with alist-right | true |
| P04f | alist(s), with alist-right | infinitely many, as P04d |

## Observations

- P04a and P04b: whether x = 1 is reported, and then whether the
  computation finishes, holds alternatives pending, suspends or runs to
  the budget.
- P04c and P04e: the outcome, and whether the computation finishes.
- P04d and P04f: which solutions are reported, in what order, and whether
  every solution would be reached given enough steps. Compare only this
  property across systems, not the number reported within the budget.
# P05. Late contradiction

**Probes:** how a system holds several alternatives while constraints that
eliminate some of them arrive, and what happens to answers it has already
given.

## Vocabulary

pick(x): a closed world of three facts, in this order: pick(1), pick(2),
pick(3).

x > 1 and x ≠ 2 are primitive comparisons.

## P05a. Choice first

| stage | information | valid outcomes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | pick(x) | x ∈ {1, 2, 3} |
| 2 | x > 1 | x ∈ {2, 3} |
| 3 | x ≠ 2 | x = 3 |

## P05b. Constraint first

| stage | information | valid outcomes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | x > 1 | every integer x > 1 |
| 2 | pick(x) | x ∈ {2, 3} |

## P05c. Contradiction

| stage | information | valid outcomes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | pick(x) | x ∈ {1, 2, 3} |
| 2 | x = 4 | none |
| 3 | x = 3 | none |

Stage 3 adds to stages that are already inconsistent, so the valid outcome
stays empty.

## Observations

- After each stage: whether every surviving alternative is held at once, or
  one is held and the others kept for backtracking, or the others are lost.
- An answer reported at one stage and invalid at the next: how its
  withdrawal is shown, if at all.
- P05b stage 1: how a comparison on an unknown is treated: held, reported
  as a residual, enumerated, or an error.
- P05c: how the empty outcome is reported, and whether stage 3 can be
  posed at all.

begin
  comment HARNESS POSING incremental;
  comment PROVENANCE author: harness-algol-60 (qualification program for a made-up problem, not a result);
  comment PROVENANCE precursor seen: no;
  comment PROVENANCE idioms: the Revised Report (1962), and the interpreter's input and output procedures;
  comment X02 (made up). Stage 1: choose p in 1..c1, the least, and emit it. Stage 2: commit to p and emit the commitment. Stage 3: p differs from c3. Constants file: a line 1: c1 and a line 3: c3. An answer is p alone, so that a replayed commitment v can be read back with ininteger;
  integer n, cap, m, i, code, k, c1, c3, p;
  ininteger(0, n); ininteger(0, cap); ininteger(0, m);
  for i := 1 step 1 until m do ininteger(0, code);
  p := 0;
  for i := 1 while true do
  begin
    ininteger(0, code); ininteger(0, k);
    if code = 3 then ininteger(0, p)
    else if k = 1 then
    begin ininteger(0, c1); if c1 >= 1 then p := 1; outstring(1, "[emit]chose "); outinteger(1, p); outstring(1, "[/emit]") end
    else if k = 2 then
    begin outstring(1, "[emit]commit "); outinteger(1, p); outstring(1, "[/emit]") end
    else if k = 3 then
    begin ininteger(0, c3); if p = c3 then p := 0 end;
    if p > 0 then begin outstring(1, "[answer]"); outinteger(1, p); outstring(1, "[/answer]") end;
    outstring(1, "\n[observe][bind p]"); outinteger(1, p); outstring(1, "[/bind][/observe]\n[end]")
  end
end

======
# The X1 dialect

`algol60 --x1` runs a program as the ALGOL 60 system of Dijkstra and
Zonneveld for the Electrologica X1 (Mathematical Centre, Amsterdam, 1960;
this is the version of about 1964) would have run it, as far as the
documents say. It is not an emulation of the X1.

## Sources

- **[KA03]** F. E. J. Kruseman Aretz, *The Dijkstra–Zonneveld ALGOL 60
  compiler for the Electrologica X1*, CWI note SEN-N0301, 2003. Section 1.3
  reproduces, in translation, the 23 "special properties of the
  MC-Algol-system" from the user manual of 12 December 1962; appendix A the
  compile-time and run-time stops; chapter 7 the library; appendix B
  Zonneveld's outer planets program.
- **[KA-X1X8]** F. E. J. Kruseman Aretz, *A comparison between the ALGOL 60
  implementations on the Electrologica X1 and the Electrologica X8*, CWI.
  Section 3.2: the representation of values. Section 3.3.3: the run-time
  code of the for statement. Appendix A, note 3: the X1's `FLOT`.
- **[X1-man]** Appendix B.1 of [KA-X1X8]: an extract, in Kruseman Aretz's
  translation, of the X1 ALGOL user manual itself (the 1964 "Load-and-go"
  system, MCP documentation P100). The only part of the X1's own manual
  found. It describes the arithmetic of the run-time complexes ALD (in
  general use) and ALS (single length, "seldom used and not maintained
  from 1963 onwards"), and lists 26 special properties, a later version of
  the 23 of [KA03, 1.3].
- **x1algol.pas**, Kruseman Aretz's Pascal version of the compiler, which
  "for a range of ALGOL 60 programs produces exactly the same object code
  as the original" [KA03, 1.5]. Its name-list prefill gives the library
  names.
- **[X8-lib]** The provisional library manual of the *X8* system, section 7
  (in translation in sergev's `doc/library-procedures.md`). The only
  description found of `PRINT`, `FIXT`, `ABSFIXT`, `FLOT`, `TAB`, `SUM`
  and `EVEN`. The X8 system came from the same institute and kept the
  names, but it is not the X1's manual.
- **[course]** E. W. Dijkstra, *Cursus programmeren in ALGOL 60*,
  Mathematical Centre, 2nd edition February 1962 (https://ir.cwi.nl/pub/9591)
  and 11th edition (https://ir.cwi.nl/pub/9606): the course for the first
  MC system, the one modelled here. Its description of `print`, of the
  range of reals, and of assignment to an integer.
- **[MR54]** P. J. J. van de Laarschot and J. Nederkoorn, *Voorlopige
  gebruiksaanwijzing van de tweede MC ALGOL 60-vertaler*, MR 54, 1963
  (https://ir.cwi.nl/pub/9230). The manual of the *second* X1 system, with
  its own complex (ALP, a real in one word), so its arithmetic is not
  evidence about this one; but "the MCP libraries of the first and the
  second ALGOL 60 translator are kept as much alike as possible, at least
  as the user sees them", and it defines `FIXT`, `FLOT`, `ABSFIXT` and
  `print`.
- **[Tract8]** J. A. Zonneveld, *Automatic Numerical Integration*,
  Mathematical Centre Tracts 8, 1964 (https://ir.cwi.nl/pub/13099): the
  outer planets program with the X1's own output
  ([`historical/README.md`](../historical/README.md)).
- **[MR55]** E. W. Dijkstra, *Objectprogramma, gegenereerd door de M.C.
  vertaler*, MR 55, 1963: the operations of the complex and the layout of
  the accumulator stack (a real there has a whole word of binary
  exponent). Nothing on the arithmetic's results.
- **[sergev]** https://github.com/sergev/x1-algol-compiler (Apache-2.0):
  the Pascal compiler, a C translation of it with three of its bugs
  documented, and a simulator that runs the compiler's object code. The
  run-time routines of the X1 (the "complex", ALD and ALS) were printed
  by the Mathematical Centre as the series P(1)200 [KA03, 1.1], and
  Kruseman Aretz typed them in again [KA03, 1.6] to rerun the system, but no copy has
  been found, so the simulator's are a reconstruction of their own. It is built in
  `sources/sergev-x1/build` and run by `compare/run.sh`; see
  [`compare/README.md`](../compare/README.md).

"Property n" is the n-th special property of [KA03, 1.3]; "stop n" is a
stop of [KA03, appendix A].

## The manual's rules are not the compiler's checks

The first version of this dialect refused programs that broke the
manual's rules. That was a misreading. [KA03, 1.3]: "The greatest
shortcoming of the system, however, was the almost complete absence of
syntax checks"; the only grammatical check was for undeclared identifiers.
And programs that break the rules compile with the real compiler: in
sergev's examples, `beer`, `disarium`, `magic_square`, `mersenne` and
`whetstone` declare procedures before variables (property 15), `lisp` and
`pentomino` put `if` after `do` (property 12), and `bulls_and_cows` has
`then if`, which even the Report forbids.

So `--x1` accepts such programs, with a warning naming the property: the
manual forbade it, the compiler did not check, and what followed is not
known. The run-time stops of appendix A (integer capacity, an array with a
lower bound above its upper) remain errors, since they really did stop the
X1.

## What changes the meaning of a program

| | The Report | The X1 | Source | Test (`tests/x1.rs`) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The step of `for V := A step B until C` | Evaluated twice each time round, after `V := A` | Once each time round, and the first time *before* `V := A` | Property 11; FOR1, FOR5–FOR7 in [KA-X1X8, 3.3.3] | `property_11_*` |
| `go to` an undefined switch designator | A dummy statement (4.3.5) | Undefined; here an error | Property 10 | `property_10_*` |
| `abs` | Real | The type of its argument | Property 6 | `property_6_*` |
| `sqrt`, `ln` of a negative number | Undefined | Of its absolute value | Property 6; [X1-man] point 6 | `property_6_*` |
| The value of a typed procedure | Converted to the declared type | "Determined by the arithmetic carried out this time" | Property 18 | `property_18_*` |
| Order of evaluating parameters called by value | Not fixed; left to right here | The order of the specifications | Property 22 | `property_22_*` |
| Identifiers | All characters count | The first nine | Property 3 | `property_3_*` |
| `0.0`, `0⏨5` | Real | Integer | Property 4 | `property_4_*` |
| Whole numbers above 67108863 | Integer | Real | Property 4 | `property_4_*` |
| A real assigned to an integer, or used as a subscript | `entier(x + 0.5)`: −2.5 gives −2 | Rounded (MR 35; [X1-man]); a half away from zero, −2.5 gives −3, which is inferred ([`decisions.md`](decisions.md)) | MR 35; [X1-man]; inference | `a_half_is_rounded_away_from_zero` |
| Integers | 64 bits here | ±67108863. An intermediate result beyond that "is transformed automatically to real representation"; assigning it to an integer is stop 1–1, using it with `÷` stop 1–8 | [KA-X1X8, 3.2]; [X1-man]; stops 1–1, 1–8 | `stop_1_1_*`, `an_integer_intermediate_*` |
| An array whose lower bound is above its upper | Has no elements | Stop 1–2 | Stop 1–2 | `stop_1_2_*` |
| Real variables, value parameters and constants | 53-bit mantissa | Rounded to 40 bits when stored ("rounded to 12 decimals"); 52 on the stack. A real constant is two words of the constant list, like a variable, so `0.1` itself has 40 bits | [KA-X1X8, 3.2]; [X1-man]; `look_for_constant` in x1algol.pas; the real compiler on x1sim | `reals_are_stored_*` |
| Zero as a real | 0 | Never 0. The integer 0 as a real, and a sum or difference that is exactly 0, are the least positive number of the stack; stored, that is the least real, about .3094⏨−616. So `a = 0` is false for every real variable `a`, `sign(a)` is 1 after `a := 0`, and `1 / 0` is not an error | [X1-man]; [KA-X1X8, 3.2] ("the value 0 being replaced by about 10⁻⁶⁰⁰") | `a_real_variable_is_never_zero` |
| A real beyond the range of variables | An error here | Stored as the greatest or least magnitude, with its sign | [X1-man] | `a_real_beyond_the_range_*` |
| `if b then if c then S else T` | Not allowed | Accepted; `else` goes with the nearest `if` | [sergev] `bulls_and_cows` | `then_if_*` |

**Rounding of stored reals.** [X1-man]: "in the complex ALD the result,
represented in the accumulator in 15 decimals relative precision, is
rounded to 12 decimals". sergev's simulator agrees: its
`FIXT(4, 17, 9999/7)` prints `1428.42857142910361289`, which is 9999/7
rounded to 40 bits; truncated it would be `1428.42857142724…`. How a value
exactly halfway between two 40-bit mantissas is rounded is not said;
`--x1` rounds it away from zero (Rust's `round`).

**The range of reals.** A variable's exponent has 12 bits, so its
magnitude lies between 2⁻²⁰⁴⁸ (about .3094⏨−616) and about .1616⏨+617; on
the stack the exponent has 27 bits. An f64 reaches neither, so `--x1` uses
stand-ins in the same order of size: the least f64 normal number for the
least real, a number below it for the stack's zero, and the greatest f64
with a 40-bit mantissa for the greatest real. A real whose decimal
exponent would exceed 600, which is all three, is printed as "the integer
0 or 'inf'" with its sign [course], at the right of the field: the X1
printed a mass of 0 as `+                  0` [Tract8, p. 106]. A result
smaller in magnitude than the stack's zero (such as `0 / 2`) is kept at
it, which is assumed. Values between 10³⁰⁸ and 10⁶¹⁶, or
between 10⁻³⁰⁸ and 10⁻⁶¹⁶, are not modelled.

A value worked out from a stand-in can leave that band. The square root of
the least real is about 1.49⏨−154 here, where the X1's would be 2⁻¹⁰²⁴,
about .556⏨−308; both are far from 0, but the digits printed are the
stand-in's, not the X1's. TPK meets this when an input is 0: `sqrt(abs(t))`
of a variable assigned 0 prints 1.49166814624004e-154 under `--x1`. Any such
number is evidence only that the result was not 0.

## The manual's rules (warnings)

| Property | Warned about |
| --- | --- |
| 5 | A standard function (`abs` ... `entier`) called as a statement |
| 12 | A conditional statement straight after `do` |
| 13 | A parameter delimiter other than a comma, such as `) Order: (` |
| 15 | Declarations other than in the order scalars, arrays, switches, procedures; specifications other than scalars and strings, arrays, labels and switches, procedures |
| 17 | Bounds that are not integer numbers, for an `own` array or one in the outermost block |
| 19 | A formal parameter without a specification |
| 21 | A label in the value list |
| [KA03, ch. 7] | `abs`, `sign`, `sqrt`, `sin`, `cos`, `ln`, `exp`, `entier`, `read`, `print`, `TAB`, `NLCR`, `SPACE` as actual parameters: operators of the run-time complex, not procedures. [sergev] documents the compiler producing bad code for some of these |

Property 8, labels that begin with a digit, is an error: the real
compiler stops with a fatal error on `10:` (`compare/probes/numeric-label.a60`).
So is property 1, a labelled program: Knuth and Trabb Pardo's TPK begins
`TPK: begin`, and the real compiler stops with 0–25, "exhausted source
store" (`compare/probes/tpk-1976.a60`).
Property 23 (a value array has at most five subscripts) is an error at the
call. Not checked: properties 2, 9, 16 and 20.

A value part after a specification (`real t; value t;`, as in TPK) is
not among the manual's properties. The Report forbids it (5.4.1), and so
does the Report dialect here. The X1 compiler accepted it but compiled t
as a value array (`compare/probes/value-after-spec.a60`), so `--x1` warns,
and calls t by value. (Knuth's errata for the 2003 reprint of the paper
correct the heading to the Report's order, 12 February 2014.)

## The library

`read`, `print`, `TAB`, `NLCR`, `SPACE`, `stop`, `SUM`, `PRINTTEXT`, `FLOT`,
`FIXT`, `ABSFIXT` and `EVEN` (the prefill of the name list in x1algol.pas),
with the meanings of [course], [MR54] and [X8-lib], checked against the
X1's own output [Tract8]:

- `print(x)`: by the type of x [course; MR54]. An integer "in at most
  eight decimals, non-significant zeros replaced by spaces", with its
  sign: `FIXT(8, 0, x)`. A real by `FLOT(13, 3, x)`, "the fraction in the
  computing precision" (13 digits is the X8's), or as 0 or `inf` beyond an
  exponent of 600. Then the start of the next column; "at most 7 columns
  are typed on a line" [course]. The X1's column width is not known; the
  X8's 21 positions are kept.
- `ABSFIXT(n, m, x)`: a space, |x| with n digits before the point and m
  after, leading zeros as spaces (the units zero too, unless m = 0), a
  space. `FIXT` puts the sign in place of the first space: "Typt teken,
  n decimale cijfers van geheel deel van x, ..." [MR54], and the X1
  printed `+ 3.429474152`, `- .049534455` [Tract8]. (The X8 manual puts
  the sign beside the first digit; this dialect did so until the X1's
  output was found.)
- `FLOT`: sign, point, mantissa between .1 and 1, ⏨, signed exponent. The
  X8's has three parameters (n, m, x). **The X1's has two**: Zonneveld's
  program calls `FLOT(12, x)`. Its exponent has two digits: "the number
  of decimals for the exponent was here fixed to two" [KA-X1X8, appendix
  A, note 3]. x1sim's `FLOT` has the same layout.
- `TAB` to the next multiple of 8 (at least 2 on), `SPACE(n)`, `NLCR`; a
  line of 144 positions, beyond which a new line is begun.
- `SUM(i, a, b, x)` and `EVEN(n)` as the manual declares them.

`XEEN`, which reads the operator's console, is not provided. The
procedures of the Modified Report (`outstring`, `outreal` ...) are kept so
that the same test programs run in both dialects; the X1 did not have
them.

## Compared with the real compiler on sergev's simulator

`compare/` runs 33 probe programs through `--x1` and through the real 1964
compiler on x1sim; [`compare/README.md`](../compare/README.md) has the
table, and says which results are decided by the compiler (and so are
evidence about the X1) and which by the run-time (two reconstructions).
In brief:

- **Confirmed by the real compiler**: value parameters evaluated in the
  order of specification (property 22), nine symbols of an identifier
  (property 3), `then if` with `else` on the nearest `if`, both operands
  of `∧` and `∨` evaluated, and programs that break the manual's rules
  compiling (properties 15 and 19; Knuth's program as printed gives −67).
- **Confirmed for the order of evaluation**: primaries left to right
  (property 7), a variable fetched before a later function call in the
  same expression changes it, subscripts left to right, and in an
  assignment the left part subscripts before the expression (Report
  4.2.3, also with several left parts). `−a↑2` is −(a↑2).
- **Corrected after it**: numeric labels make the compiler fail, so `--x1`
  refuses them; real constants are stored in 40 bits, so `0.1 - 0.1`
  stored is 0.
- **Zonneveld's outer planets** through the real compiler: all 88 numbers
  printed agree with `--x1`.
- **The run-times disagree** on `abs` of an integer and `sqrt` of a
  negative number (x1sim against property 6, which `--x1` follows). On
  rounding −2.5 to an integer they now agree (−3), by an inference from
  the X1's ones' complement arithmetic, its compiler's rounding and the
  X8 ([`decisions.md`](decisions.md)).
- **Where the X1 user manual [X1-man] decides against x1sim**: a real
  variable set to 0 is not equal to 0 and has sign 1, `1 / 0` is not an
  error, an integer intermediate beyond 67108863 is real, and `ln` takes
  the absolute value. x1sim does what a modern machine does in each
  case.

Its 22 example programs were also run with `--x1` and compared with the
outputs its README and tests record:

- **The same values**: `man_or_boy` (−67), `disarium`, `magic_square`,
  `mersenne`, `perfect_numbers`, `palindromic_primes`, `sieve` (78498
  primes below a million), `steady_squares`, `sum`, `hanoi`, `hello`.
- **Zonneveld's outer planets** (`historical/jaz164.alg`, with sergev's
  input data): all 45 coordinates after integrating over 1000 days agree
  to the nine decimals printed. (One differed in the last digit until
  real constants were stored in 40 bits.)
- **`FIXT`, `ABSFIXT`, `FLOT`**: the digits of all of sergev's test cases
  agree, including those that show the 40-bit store. The last printed
  digit differs once, where sergev truncates and the manual says the
  number "is rounded exactly to the last decimal place".
- **Layout, where the two readings differ**:
  - `FIXT`: both put the sign in the first column (`-  57`), as the X1
    did [Tract8]; here it was beside the first digit until that output
    was found.
  - `FIXT` with decimals: sergev keeps the units zero (`- 0.049534455`);
    here it is suppressed (`-  .049534455`), as on the X1 [Tract8].
  - `print`: sergev's is a convenience (compact, several arguments); here
    it is the course's: eight positions for an integer, `FLOT` for a
    real.
- **Not run here**: programs using `PRSYM`, `RESYM` and `TIMEOFDAY`
  (sergev's library has them; the 1964 compiler's name list does not),
  `whetstone` (sergev's several-argument `print`), `sqrt_test` (an X8
  program, with the X8's `FLOT`), `bulls_and_cows` (a missing `;` that the
  real compiler let through), `pentomino` (needs its input).
- **Not modelled here**: reals between about 10³⁰⁸ and the X1's 10⁶¹⁶
  (sergev's tests use them; only the ends of the range are modelled, see
  "The range of reals"), and the X1's negative zero (it used ones'
  complement; sergev's `FIXT(3, 0, -0.0)` prints `-  0`).

## Results so far

- **`evaluation-count`**: the step is evaluated 11 times on the X1, 21 by
  the Report, for ten times round.
- **`jensen`**: H(100) is 5.18737751763547 on the X1 and 5.18737751763962
  by the Report; the running sum is cut to 40 bits every time it is
  stored.
- **`man-or-boy-1964`**, Knuth's program as printed: its parameters `x1`
  ... `x5` are unspecified, against property 19. The real compiler
  accepts it anyway, and gives −67 (`compare/probes/man-or-boy-unspecified.a60`),
  as `--x1` does.
- **`x1-probes`** differs on every line: properties 11, 22, 18 and 3, and
  the 40-bit store.
- **Koster's jungle generator** (CWI software archive) uses `RANDOM`,
  `SETRANDOM` and `XEEN`, none in the 1964 library; it mentions "the world
  famous X8 Computer". With the three declared, it runs.

## Running the real thing

The compiler survives; the run-time complex does not, as far as is
public. [KA03, 1.6]: Kruseman Aretz "wrote an X1 emulator, typed in the
complex of run–time support routines, and was so able to rerun the X1
ALGOL 60 system", but published neither.

- **Van den Hove's thesis** (2019) has a chapter III in two parts,
  "Translating ALGOL 60 Programs" and "Executing ALGOL 60 Programs", on an
  ISO C version of the system reverse-engineered from its assembler, and
  an appendix G, "Getting and Using the System". Only the front matter,
  contents and appendices A and B are public (UvA DARE); the author holds
  the rest for a book. The address it gives for current information,
  http://www.fibonacci.org/GHE3, did not answer on 23 November 2026. If
  the C version includes the run-time complex, the rows of the first table
  can be checked against the original routines. The author is the person
  to ask.
- **sergev's simulator** is built and in use (`compare/`). It answers
  every question the compiler decides. For the run-time it is a second
  reconstruction, not the original.

content.content:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""ALGOL 60 syntax check, which executes nothing (harnesses/algol-60/README.md, 'check').

    harnesses/algol-60/check CONFIGURATION PROGRAM

report : algol60 --check PROGRAM          (compiles; reports errors and warnings)
x1     : algol60 --x1 --check PROGRAM     (the same, in the X1 dialect)
x1sim  : x1algc PROGRAM x1algol.lib       (the X1 compiler alone, in a fresh temporary
                                           directory; its object code is discarded and
                                           x1sim, the simulator, is never started)

It also reads the program's bytes for the harness's own declaration
(HARNESS POSING incremental|reposed). The system's messages are printed
verbatim. Exit status: 0 no error reported; 1 an error was reported;
2 usage error.
"""

import os
import re
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile

ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))))


def main(argv):
    if len(argv) != 3 or argv[1] not in ("report", "x1", "x1sim"):
        sys.stderr.write(__doc__)
        return 2
    config, prog = argv[1], argv[2]
    path = prog if os.path.isabs(prog) else os.path.join(ROOT, prog)
    if not os.path.isfile(path):
        sys.stderr.write("check: no program at %s\n" % prog)
        return 2
    rel = os.path.relpath(path, ROOT)
    ok = True
    text = open(path, "rb").read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
    decl = set(re.findall(r"HARNESS\s+POSING\s+(incremental|reposed)", text))
    if len(decl) == 1:
        print("harness: posing declared: %s" % decl.pop())
    else:
        print("harness: ERROR: the program must declare exactly one of 'HARNESS POSING incremental' "
              "or 'HARNESS POSING reposed' in a comment (found %s)" % (sorted(decl) or "none"))
        ok = False
    const = os.path.splitext(path)[0] + ".constants"
    print("harness: constants file: %s" % (os.path.relpath(const, ROOT) if os.path.isfile(const) else "none"))
    env = {"PATH": "/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin", "LC_ALL": "C.UTF-8"}
    tmp = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="algol60-check-")
    env["HOME"] = tmp
    try:
        if config in ("report", "x1"):
            cmd = ["/usr/local/bin/algol60"] + (["--x1"] if config == "x1" else []) + ["--check", rel]
            print("system: %s" % " ".join(cmd))
            r = subprocess.run(cmd, cwd=ROOT, env=env, capture_output=True, timeout=120)
            sys.stdout.write(r.stdout.decode("utf-8", errors="replace"))
            sys.stdout.write(r.stderr.decode("utf-8", errors="replace"))
            print("system: exit status %d" % r.returncode)
            ok = ok and r.returncode == 0
        else:
            shutil.copyfile(path, os.path.join(tmp, "prog.a60"))
            cmd = ["/usr/local/bin/x1algc", "prog.a60", "/usr/local/lib/x1algol.lib"]
            print("system: %s  (in a temporary directory; standard output, the object code, is kept "
                  "only to show the compiler's messages when it fails)" % " ".join(cmd))
            with open(os.path.join(tmp, "prog.x1"), "wb") as obj:
                r = subprocess.run(cmd, cwd=tmp, env=env, stdout=obj, stderr=subprocess.PIPE, timeout=120)
            sys.stdout.write(r.stderr.decode("utf-8", errors="replace"))
            if r.returncode != 0:
                # x1algc writes its error report on standard output, after any object code
                out = open(os.path.join(tmp, "prog.x1"), "rb").read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
                sys.stdout.write(out)
            else:
                n = sum(1 for _ in open(os.path.join(tmp, "prog.x1"), "rb"))
                print("system: compiled; %d lines of object code discarded, not run" % n)
            print("system: exit status %d" % r.returncode)
            print("note: the X1 compiler detects fewer errors than algol60 --check; a program it accepts "
                  "can still stop at run time")
            ok = ok and r.returncode == 0
    finally:
        shutil.rmtree(tmp, ignore_errors=True)
    return 0 if ok else 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main(sys.argv))

# ALGOL 60 programs, wave 1: batch 1A (P01–P03), batch 1B (P04–P08) and batch 1C (P09–P12)

*Batch 1B and batch 1C have their own sections, [below](#batch-1b-p04p08) and [after it](#batch-1c-p09p12). What follows up to batch 1B is batch 1A's, unchanged.*
